evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry lists one small-seal example, six Chu bamboo-and-silk examples, and one item under “Other”; it lists no bronze or oracle examples for 穿. It reports the Shuowen analysis 从牙在穴中 and glosses the core sense as boring through or perforating. The entry also gives later examples for excavation, passage, threading, holes, graves, waterways, a tea vessel, and worn or broken. These are source-reported forms and sense attestations; the list alone does not establish their semantic chronology.

evidence.source: 說文解字 online and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry glosses 穿 as 通也, explains the graph as 牙 within 穴, and gives 昌緣切. Duan Yucai quotes the Shijing line about a mouse boring through a wall. This records a traditional paleographic explanation; it does not independently prove the graph’s original motivation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「穿」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites Shijing, Shao Nan, Xing Lu for piercing a wall; Huainanzi and Guangyun for threading or passing through; Han shu for digging a canal; Tang poetry for wearing clothes; and Gongyang zhuan and Zhuangzi for worn or broken. These citations show distinct documented uses, but do not by themselves establish a precise sequence or semantic derivation among them. The entry labels the received form as 穴-04-09 and provides the received Shuowen explanation.
evidence.title: A02957 穿 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: Dong Chinese treats 穴 and 牙 as meaning components, with 穴 indicating a hole and 牙 a tooth, and describes the original sense as boring a hole. It gives Mandarin chuān, Middle Chinese tsyhwen, and Old Chinese *tʰo[n] for 穿. This is a secondary dictionary account; it supplies no separate same-system reconstructions for 穴 and 牙 that would establish a phonetic role for either component.
evidence.title: 穿 — Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry gives modern Mandarin chuān; Guangyun fanqie 昌緣 and 尺絹; level and departing tone categories; and Middle Chinese divisions for those readings. It cites Shijing for piercing, Liji for digging, Lunheng for passing through, Wenxin diaolong for threading or joining, and later sources for holes, graves, waterways, a tea implement, and worn or broken senses. The example sequence is not proof of a chronological chain.

gaps: The source references inspected here provide no oracle-bone or bronze forms for 穿. This is a limit of the consulted entry, not proof none exist.

Shuowen’s tooth-in-hole analysis is a received historical explanation. The dossier’s competing Chu-script account involving an 耳/串 spelling and later confusion is not independently resolved by the pages successfully inspected in this invocation.

The early disputed manuscript reading (穿, 貫, or a graph associated with 聯) and the proposed phonetic reassignment remain uncertain. The cited specialist discussion in the dossier is not new verification in this invocation.

No component-specific modern and same-system historical pronunciation comparison for 穴 and 牙 was established. The available entry gives readings for 穿 but does not show evidence that either component functions phonetically; the semantic-component account is supported as a source assertion, while the alternative remains unverified here.

The earliest text located in the dossier is the received pre-Qin Shijing corpus; the poem’s precise composition date is not established by the pages inspected here. Later dictionary citations attest senses separately but do not establish each semantic bridge or chronology.

No historical glyph image candidate met the requirement for verified identity, inspectable description, direct image URL, and reuse provenance. The CUHK linked images were inaccessible or empty; Commons searches/open attempts failed to establish a 穿 file. The text-only form catalogue provides no image reuse rights.

limitations.text: No candidate image is proposed because inspected searches and source pages did not establish an image of 穿 with both verifiable identity and reusable rights. The CUHK catalogue reports small-seal, Chu manuscript, and other forms, but the linked image resources could not be inspected or assigned reuse terms here; Commons attempts surfaced only unrelated character files.
